t.jinfoshan karst@29.0,107.2:
Jinfo Mountain rises out of the humid hills of southern Chongqing like a lump of dark green stone, its summit around twenty-two hundred metres, ringed by sheer limestone cliffs that fall for hundreds of metres in places. The name means Golden Buddha, and the story is that at sunset the cliffs of the peak catch the last light and take on the colour and shape of a seated figure. The mountain is a tableland, a block of limestone lifted high and sliced by weather, and the top is covered in clouds for much of the year, in a world of mist, bamboo, moss and rhododendron.

UNESCO lists Jinfoshan as part of the South China Karst, a vast area of limestone landscapes with towers, caves, gorges and sinkholes that was inscribed in stages. A large number of rare plants and animals live on the mountain, including several kinds of monkey, which are sometimes seen from the paths. To the north-east lies Wulong, another part of the same listing, with natural bridges and a sinkhole of staggering size called Qingkou Giant Doline, the kind of spot used as a film location for the Hollywood blockbusters.

The mountain roads of Chongqing are exciting. They climb in steep, repeated switchbacks through forest, with hairpins every hundred metres or so and a rail only on the worst drops, and then run along the edge of plateaus with long views across a sea of cloud. Surface quality varies widely, with fresh asphalt in some stretches and potholes, mud and rockfall in others, and rain falls frequently, so the roads are often wet. Fog is dense in the morning. Summer can be hot and humid, but the mountain stays cool, and the best times are spring and autumn.

Puhechang is a hamlet of about sixteen hundred people some thirty-six kilometres away, so do not count on fuel there. Fill up in a larger town, such as Nanchuan or Wulong, before heading into the hills. Food is the sharp, numbing, chilli-laden cooking of Chongqing, famous for hotpot. Foreign riders in China face strict rules about licences, plates and guides, so check the situation beforehand, and bring a waterproof layer because the mountain makes its own weather.
t.beishan cliffside carvings@29.7,105.7:
Beishan is a hill above the town of Dazu in Chongqing, and its cliff is one of the finest galleries of Buddhist sculpture in China. Beginning in the late Tang dynasty, in the ninth century, a local official ordered carvings into the rock face, and over the next two and a half centuries the work grew into a long wall of niches, with figures of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, monks and guardians, carved with extraordinary refinement. It is part of the Dazu Rock Carvings, which UNESCO listed in 1999.

What sets Beishan apart is its delicacy. The figures are slender and graceful, with soft robes, detailed jewellery and calm expressions, and many of them were once painted and gilded. The Water-Moon Guanyin, the goddess of mercy sitting in a relaxed pose, with a gentle face and a flowing robe, is among the best-known pieces, and the Peacock King, a fierce protector riding a bird, shows the same skill. The carvings are in shallow niches along a covered gallery, so you walk close to them, and the air has a mixture of incense and damp stone.

The Sichuan basin is a green, misty country. Hills are covered with terraced rice fields, bamboo groves and small farms, and the weather is often cloudy and damp, which is part of the reason the carvings are weathered in places. The hill itself is wooded, with camphor and cypress trees, and the carved wall catches the soft light. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and in summer the air is humid and hot.

For the rider, the roads of Chongqing are a mix of modern expressways and winding country lanes, and they are crowded with trucks and scooters. Foreign visitors who want to ride in China should check the rules for licences and registration before travel, since they are strict. Dazu has fuel stations, hotels and restaurants, and the town centre is a short walk from the site. Sichuan food is hot and numbing, with chilli and pepper, and a bowl of noodles or a hot pot is the right reward after a morning among the carvings. Early mornings are quietest.
t.dazu rock carvings@29.7,105.7:
Dazu is the place where a medieval Buddhist vision was carved on a human scale, and the surprise is how alive it still feels. Across the hills around the town in Chongqing, more than seventy sites hold carvings from the ninth to the thirteenth centuries, made in the late Tang and Song dynasties, when a local community of monks, officials and lay believers turned the soft red sandstone into a theatre of faith. UNESCO recognised the group in 1999. Visitors usually see two main sites, Beishan and Baodingshan, and they make a pair.

Baodingshan is the larger and the more dramatic. The work was planned by a monk named Zhao Zhifeng in the twelfth century and covers a horseshoe-shaped valley, with a long cliff face carved into a vast tableau of Buddhist and everyday scenes. There are hell scenes and heavenly scenes, a huge wheel of life held by a demon, and a reclining Buddha thirty metres long, whose body seems to disappear into the rock. The carvings show not only gods but ordinary people: farmers, nursing mothers, cattle herders, and a woman feeding chickens, as if the sculptors were deliberately mixing the sacred and the everyday.

The setting is the Sichuan basin, a lush, humid country of terraced fields, bamboo and camphor trees, often wrapped in mist. The cliffs are under a roof of overhanging rock and have survived better than you would expect in such a wet climate, partly thanks to careful drainage built into the original design. The best light is in the early morning, before the tour groups arrive, and in autumn the air is clearer.

For the rider, the region is hilly and green, with busy roads, trucks, scooters and farm traffic. Visitors who want to ride in China must check the rules on licences and registration, which are strict and change often. Dazu has fuel, hotels and plenty of restaurants, and the carved sites are a short drive from the town. Sichuan cooking is bold, with chilli and Sichuan pepper that makes the lips tingle, and it is worth ordering a dish you cannot identify. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.djupivogur@64.7,-14.3:
Djúpivogur is a fishing village on the south-east coast of Iceland, tucked into a bay on the Berufjörður fjord, and it has the sort of quiet confidence that comes from knowing exactly what it is. Behind it rises Búlandstindur, a steep, pyramid-shaped mountain just over a thousand metres high, which dominates the skyline and gets its share of folklore. On the waterfront, there is a line of large stone eggs set on little plinths in the shallows, a sculpture by the artist Sigurður Guðmundsson that represents the nesting birds of the area, and it is the kind of public art that gets you smiling before you have taken off your helmet.

The riding is the point. Route 1, the Ring Road, follows the coast along a string of deep fjords, with the road swinging out to each headland and in again to the head of the fjord, so that you travel three times as far as the crow flies. The bends are open and the views are enormous, with steep slopes of scree, waterfalls streaming down in wet weather, and the sea shining below. Winds can be fierce, especially where the road crosses the mouth of a fjord, and in winter the whole route needs care. Long stretches are now paved, but there are still some gravel patches and roadworks to watch for.

The village is a member of the Cittaslow movement, which promotes a slower, more local way of life, and it has the feel of it. There is a small harbour, a few shops, and an old trading warehouse that has been turned into a cafe and museum. A short walk gives you views over the bay full of birds, including eider ducks, and in the right season you may see seals on the skerries. The fish served in the local restaurants is as fresh as you will find anywhere, usually landed the same day.

Fuel is available here, with a small station in the village, but it is wise to keep your tank above half in the east, since the distances between settlements are large and some pumps are unmanned or card-only. There is also a campsite, guesthouses and a hotel.

The best time to come is June to August, when the days are long and the road is clear. In the evening the light on the fjord can be extraordinary, and the sun on the mountain turns the rock a deep rose.
t.breiddalsvik@64.8,-14.0:
Some places announce themselves and some just happen to you. Breiðdalsvík is the second kind, a handful of houses by a wide, shallow bay at the mouth of the Breiðdalur valley in eastern Iceland, with a harbour that still works and a population you could fit in a village hall. The valley behind it opens out between mountains that are some of the oldest rock in the country, laid down by volcanoes more than ten million years ago, and geologists have been coming here for decades because the layers are so clearly exposed. A small geology centre in the old co-operative building keeps that tradition going, which is an unusually serious thing to find in a place this size.

The ride here follows the coast road along the southern fjords of the east, a route that does not get the attention the Ring Road does. It is a quiet, unhurried drive. The road winds around headlands and across river mouths, climbing and falling in modest bends, with the sea on one side and bare, streaked slopes on the other, and you will often go for ten minutes without meeting anything. If you come over from Egilsstaðir, the high shortcut across Öxi is a gravel mountain road that is not suitable for everyone and is closed in winter, so most riders stick to the coast.

Wind and weather are the variables. Even in July the east can produce fog that sits low on the water and drizzle that arrives sideways, and in the same hour the sun can break through and light up the green valley floor. Sheep stray onto the road. Surfaces are mostly paved but there are gravel patches and the occasional stretch where frost heave has left bumps. Slow down on the fjord roads and use your lights.

For practicalities, services here are thin. There is a guesthouse or two, a small cafe in season, and a brewery attached to a local bar that makes a fair bid to be the area's social centre, but you should not rely on opening hours outside summer. Fuel is the main concern. The nearest dependable supplies are in Djúpivogur to the south, or Reyðarfjörður and Egilsstaðir to the north, and the distances are long enough that it is worth filling before you commit.

Stop on the shore if you have time. The beach is dark, the air is sharp with salt and seaweed, and eiders and gulls work the shallows. It is a good place to sit on the bike for a while and realise how few people you have seen all day.
t.wulong karst three natural bridges@29.4,:
In Wulong, in the mountains of Chongqing, the rock is the architecture. The karst here, a limestone landscape of caves, gorges and sinkholes, has been carved by water over millions of years into huge forms, among them three natural bridges, giant stone arches that span a river gorge. Tianlong, Qinglong and Heilong bridges, each one rising well over a hundred metres, with spans of tens of metres, are among the biggest natural bridges in the world, and the river runs beneath them, in forest so deep that the light is green.

The area is part of the South China Karst, which UNESCO listed in 2007 and extended later. Wulong's other features include Furong Cave, a huge cave system with rimstone pools and calcite formations, and the Qingkou Giant Doline, a collapse sinkhole big enough to hold a small village. The scale was a draw for filmmakers, and the landscape has appeared in several international films. The surrounding countryside is a mix of forest, terraced fields and mountain pasture, with hamlets of wooden houses, and the air is cooler than in Chongqing, which is famously hot in summer, so city people come here to escape.

The roads in the area are mountain roads with tight bends, steep gradients and fog, and they pass through small valleys where you meet farmers on motorbikes and trucks carrying goods. The surface is generally good, but landslides can occur after heavy rain, and visibility can drop suddenly in the mist. Autumn is the best season, with clear skies and colour in the trees, and spring brings blossom and frequent rain. Check for road conditions before starting, and allow extra time, because distances are deceptive.

There are no larger towns on our list near here, so rely on Wulong's county town for fuel, shops and restaurants, and carry water and snacks when you go into the park. The food in Chongqing and the surrounding region is famously spicy, with chillies and Sichuan pepper, and a meal in a village will give you a taste. Tickets to the main sights are sold at the entrances, and some paths involve steps and boat or lift rides, so expect to walk.
t.shimenshan cliffside carvings@29.7,105.9:
Shimenshan is one of the clusters of rock carvings around Dazu, in Chongqing, where sandstone cliffs were turned into sacred art between the ninth and thirteenth centuries. The Dazu Rock Carvings, a UNESCO listing since 1999, include several sites: Beishan with its small niches, Baodingshan with its sweeping Buddhist tableaux, and Shimenshan, Nanshan and Shizhuanshan, each with its own character. At Shimenshan the carvings, made in the Song dynasty, blend Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian figures, something rare at a single site.

What makes the place memorable is the ordinary human detail in the stone. Carvers gave their figures expressive faces, flowing robes and a sense of movement, and some scenes show everyday life, with farmers, animals and families. The cliffs sit in a green, humid landscape of red sandstone hills, bamboo groves and terraced fields. Moss grows over parts of the carvings, and water seeps through the rock, so conservation is a constant struggle.

The nearest town of any size is Yongchuan, about thirty kilometres away, with nearly ninety-five thousand people and the usual fuel stations, hotels and noodle shops. Chongqing cuisine is famously fiery, with hot pot, spicy noodles and numbing Sichuan pepper, so order accordingly. The surrounding roads wind through hills and small farms, and the traffic is a lively mix of lorries, motorbikes and electric scooters.

A practical note: motorcycle touring in China is tightly regulated, with licensing, vehicle registration and expressway restrictions that make independent riding difficult for foreigners, so plan with a local operator or a guide. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the skies are clearer and the temperature is mild. Summers are hot and sticky, and winters damp and grey, with mist hanging over the hills. Take your time at the cliffs and let your eyes adjust to the detail: the longer you look, the more figures emerge from the stone, and the whole hillside starts to feel populated. Early morning, before the tour groups arrive, is quietest, and a light drizzle, which is common here, makes the sandstone glow a deeper red and brings out the colour of the surviving paint.
t.wulong karst furong cave@29.2,107.9:
Wulong lies in the folded mountains of southeastern Chongqing, where the Wu river has carved its way through limestone for millions of years, and the result is among the most dramatic karst landscapes in China. It forms part of the South China Karst, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the area includes Furong Cave, the Three Natural Bridges and the Qingkou Giant Doline, a sinkhole so large that it holds a forest inside it. The scale of everything is hard to take in until you stand at the edge.

Furong Cave, named after the river that flows past its mouth, is one of the longest and most elaborate show caves in the region, with huge chambers, calcite flows, stalagmites and strange formations lit in colour. It was formed over a very long time by water working through the rock. The three bridges, Tianlong, Qinglong and Heilong, are natural limestone arches spanning gorges, with the river running deep below. The ground around is a maze of sinkholes, caves and steep, forested valleys.

Wulong has a county town with fuel stations and hotels, but the back roads between the sights are long and empty, so start with a full tank and carry some margin. The mountain roads in this region are twisting and steep, often cut into cliff faces, with tunnels and bridges, and fog is common. Surfaces are generally paved, though landslides after heavy rain can close sections. Fast and slow traffic mix freely, so ride with a margin.

As elsewhere in China, riding a motorcycle independently as a foreigner is heavily restricted, so plan with a licensed operator. The best times to visit are spring and autumn, when the air is clearer and the valleys are green or gold. In summer the plateau above, with its alpine meadows, is a cool escape from the heat of Chongqing, and locals flock there. Food is spicy, often with smoked meat, wild mushrooms and strong tea, and the evenings are cool and quiet.
t.nanshan cliffside carvings@29.7,105.7:
Most visitors to Dazu go for the big Buddhist panels at Baodingshan, but the carvings at Nanshan, on a wooded hillside south of the old county town in Chongqing, are a different thing: Taoist, quieter and much less visited. They belong to the same family of sites, the Dazu Rock Carvings, which UNESCO listed in 1999, and they date from the Song dynasty, roughly the twelfth century, when this part of the Sichuan basin was a centre of religious art.

The figures are cut into a cliff face under a natural overhang, protected from the worst of the rain. The most striking group is the hall of the Three Pure Ones, the highest deities of Taoism, whose calm faces look out from niches, surrounded by attendants, officials and guardians with flowing robes. The carving is fine and detailed, with the folds of the clothing, the beards and the headdresses cut with real delicacy. Traces of the original paint can still be seen in places, and in the damp green light under the trees, the stone has a soft, lived-in look.

The landscape is lush and subtropical, with bamboo, camphor trees and terraced fields, and the humid climate means the cliffs are often wet and mossy. Mist is common in the morning. Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild weather and clearer air. Summers are hot and sticky, and winters are grey and damp.

Honestly, this is not easy motorcycle country for a foreign visitor. Riding rules in China are strict, and foreign riders usually need local licensing and registered vehicles, so many people reach Dazu by bus or hired car from Chongqing, which is about a hundred and fifty kilometres to the east. Roads in the area are good, with a fast expressway and winding local roads through the hills. Try the local spicy dishes, with Sichuan pepper and chilli, and be ready for the heat. Early in the day, you may have the cliff almost to yourself.
t.wulong karst qingkou giant doline@29.6,1:
The ground drops away without warning. At Qingkou, in the hills of Wulong in the south of Chongqing, the forest opens onto a hole in the earth so large that you can hardly believe it: a giant doline, or sinkhole, hundreds of metres across and deep enough to swallow a skyscraper. Karst country is full of such things, because limestone dissolves in rainwater, and over millions of years, caves and tunnels have collapsed to create these enormous pits.

Wulong is part of the South China Karst, a UNESCO World Heritage Site first listed in 2007 and extended in 2014. It is one of the finest karst landscapes in the world, a region of natural bridges, canyons, caves and sinkholes, set in steep, forested hills. Nearby, the Three Natural Bridges, huge stone arches spanning a river gorge, have been used as a film location, and the Furong Cave is a vast cavern with underground rivers and strange formations. The scale of everything is hard to describe.

The surrounding country is green and damp, with terraced farms, villages of grey brick and tile, and mist that clings to the valleys. Maize, tobacco and vegetables are grown on every available patch of flat ground, and local farmers have a hard, steady life. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot summers and mild winters. Spring and autumn are the best seasons to visit, when the air is clear and the forest is bright.

For riders, the roads here are well built but twisty, climbing and dropping through the hills with many bends, tunnels and viaducts. Rain and fog reduce visibility, and trucks and minibuses use the same lanes. Honestly, foreign motorcycle travel in China requires special permits and local registration, and most visitors arrive by bus or hired car from Chongqing. If you are able to ride, plan fuel carefully, because stations in the mountains can be far apart, and fill up in larger towns such as Wulong county seat. Food is Sichuan-style and spicy, and local guesthouses offer simple rooms. Allow plenty of time for the paths down to the doline, and wear shoes with good grip.
t.shizhuanshan cliffside carvings@29.6,105:
Dazu is a quiet, green corner of the Chongqing hills, a long way from the skyscraper image the municipality usually gets. The Shizhuanshan carvings sit in the countryside south-west of the old town, cut into a sandstone cliff beneath trees, and they belong to the same group of Song-dynasty sites that earned Dazu a place on the World Heritage list in 1999. They are smaller and more intimate than the better-known Baodingshan, and many visitors say they are the more peaceful of the two.

What makes Shizhuanshan unusual is the mixture. Elsewhere in China, cliff carvings tend to be Buddhist, but here Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian figures share the rock, a reminder that in the twelfth century these traditions were comfortable neighbours. The sculptors worked in a soft, fine-grained stone that took detail well, and some of the figures still carry traces of colour, which gives them an almost human presence in the shade.

The roads that reach Dazu are not mountain roads in the alpine sense. They run through rolling terraces of rice, rapeseed and bamboo, with red soil, villages strung along the lanes and a lot of local traffic: motorbikes, three-wheelers, trucks and the odd water buffalo. Corners are frequent but mostly gentle, the surface varies from smooth new tarmac to patched old asphalt, and in the wet season a thin film of mud can find its way onto the bends. Ride at a conversational pace and you will see more.

The weather in this part of Sichuan basin country is often hazy and humid, and the best conditions come in spring and autumn, when the air clears a little and the temperature is kind. Summer is hot and sticky, and winter can be damp and grey, but that grey light suits a visit to a carved cliff. There is no town of any size in the immediate area, so plan your fuel and food in Dazu itself, where you will find the usual range of noodle shops and hotpot restaurants, because this is Chongqing territory and spice is part of the local language.

Take a few minutes to look at the faces on the rock before you leave. They were carved nearly a thousand years ago for ordinary worshippers, and they still look like they know who is looking at them.
Of all the stone carvings in China, the ones at Baodingshan are the most surprising, because they are not tucked into a cave but laid out like a huge outdoor theatre in a horseshoe-shaped valley. This is the best-known part of the Dazu Rock Carvings, in the hills of Chongqing, about fifteen kilometres from the old county town, and it was largely the work of one monk, Zhao Zhifeng, who spent decades in the twelfth century turning a valley into a sermon in stone.

The most famous scenes are the Wheel of Life, held in the jaws of a great figure, and a giant reclining Buddha whose body seems to run for the length of the cliff, with only the upper part visible. What makes the site so fascinating is the narrative: hell scenes, filial piety, parents and children, and ordinary people, carved with such care that it feels like a comic strip for the illiterate. Drainage channels were cut into the rock to protect the carvings from the rain, and that engineering is a big part of why they survived.

The landscape around Dazu is a low, folded patchwork of paddy, bamboo and small farms. The riding is gentle, with slow bends over red-soil country, narrow lanes where locals walk and chat, and plenty of small villages. Surfaces vary, and the rain turns some side roads slick, so take your time. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summer is hot and humid and the winter mist can be cold and grey.

You will not find much in the way of services at the carvings themselves beyond tourist stalls, so fill the tank in Dazu before you head out and eat there as well, since this is the heart of Chongqing hotpot country. The local dishes are generous with chilli and the Sichuan peppercorn that numbs the lips, so order carefully if you do not fancy a challenge.

On the same ride, Baodingshan makes a good pair with Shizhuanshan, which is a smaller and quieter site. Together they give you a sense of how the same stone culture produced both the grand public statement and the personal, almost private one.
t.ulaanbaatar@47.9,106.9:
Ulaanbaatar is the coldest national capital in the world, and it sits in a valley at about thirteen hundred and fifty metres, surrounded by bare hills, with the Tuul River running along its southern edge. About eight hundred and fifty thousand people live here, nearly half the country's population, in a mix of Soviet-era apartment blocks, glass towers and the ger districts that spread up the hillsides, where families live in felt tents with a stove and a fence. In winter, coal smoke fills the valley, and temperatures drop to minus thirty or lower.

The city has a few treasures. Gandantegchinlen Monastery, a working Buddhist monastery that survived the purges of the 1930s, has a huge gilded statue of Avalokiteshvara, and the monks' chanting in the morning is a haunting sound. Sukhbaatar Square, ringed by government buildings, has a huge seated statue of Genghis Khan, and the Zaisan memorial on a hilltop gives a view over the whole valley. The Naadam festival, in July, with wrestling, archery and horse racing, is the great national event, and the whole city goes to the stadium.

The ride from here goes north, into the green hills of the Selenge region, toward Noyon Uul, a mountain range where the Xiongnu, the nomadic confederation that rivalled the Han Chinese two thousand years ago, buried their elite. A Russian expedition opened some of the tombs in 1924 and found astonishing things: felt wall hangings, embroidered textiles, Chinese silk and lacquerware, and a Greek-style tapestry, showing the reach of the steppe's trade. The road north is paved as far as Darkhan, a fast, straight run across open steppe with huge skies, and the side tracks are gravel.

Traffic in Ulaanbaatar itself is dreadful, with jams that last for hours, so leave very early. Fuel is available in the city and in the main towns along the road, but stations are far apart in the countryside, so fill whenever you can. Mongolia drives on the right, in theory, though many vehicles have the steering wheel on the right, which makes overtaking tricky. Summer is the best season, with green grass, though thunderstorms can be sudden.
t.noyon uul s khujirt@48.5,106.6:
Khujirt is the name given to one of the quiet valleys in the folds of Noyon Uul, a range of forested hills in northern Mongolia where the horizon is all grass and sky. Hidden among the larch and birch on the slopes are the burial mounds of the Xiongnu, the nomadic empire that dominated the steppe from about the third century BC to the first century AD and troubled the Han dynasty of China. The tombs, which number over two hundred in the area, were dug deep, lined with timber and covered with a low mound of stones, and some of them are the graves of very important people.

When Russian archaeologists excavated several of the mounds in 1924, they found that the permafrost had preserved objects that would normally have rotted away. Silk embroidered with birds and flowers came from China, wool textiles with Greek and Central Asian motifs came from the west, and there were carved felt rugs showing animals fighting, a Chinese lacquered cup and a chariot. Together they show how rich the steppe elite were and how far the Silk Road reached. The finds are mostly in museums in St Petersburg and Ulaanbaatar, but the landscape remains.

Getting to the valley is part of the adventure. From Ulaanbaatar, you take the paved road north toward Darkhan, then turn off onto gravel tracks that run over rolling hills, with herds of horses, sheep and goats grazing, and gers scattered on the slopes. The tracks are not signed, and the surface can be rough, muddy after rain and dusty in dry weather, so check your route, carry a GPS and ask herders for directions. Rivers have to be crossed in places, and rain can make them impassable.

The nearest sizeable town, Dzuunharaa, about thirty-four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and simple restaurants, and it is the place to fill before heading into the hills. Carry spare fuel, food, water and warm clothes. If a herder invites you into a ger, accept a bowl of salty milk tea and some dried curds, which is the custom. Summer evenings are long and cool, and the stars are astonishing.
t.noyon uul s zuramt@48.6,106.5:
Zuramt is another of the valleys that open off Noyon Uul, and it feels a little wilder than its neighbours. The slopes on the north side of each hill are covered in dark larch and pine, while the south sides are open grass, and the pattern gives the whole range a striped, patchwork look. Streams run down through meadows full of wildflowers in June and July, with edelweiss, gentians and wild onions, and the air smells of thyme and woodsmoke. This is a land of nomadic herders, who move their animals between summer and winter pastures, and in the valleys you will see the round white gers, the horses tethered outside and the wooden frames for drying cheese.

The tombs of the Xiongnu lie hidden in the area, as they do throughout the range. They are marked by shallow square depressions in the ground, often among trees, and to the untrained eye they look like nothing, which is partly why they survived. The people here have lived among them for generations and treat them with a certain wariness. An ovoo, a cairn of stones and sticks, stands at the high point of each pass, and travellers walk around it three times clockwise and add a stone, to ask for a safe journey. It is a good custom to follow.

The riding is demanding and wonderful. Tracks follow the valley floors, with fords, soft patches and steep, rocky climbs, and in wet weather the clay becomes treacherous. Navigation is by compass and landmark rather than signposts, so go with a guide or a good map, and ride with others if you can. Weather swings from hot sun to hail in an afternoon, and dogs guarding the herds can be aggressive, so slow down when you pass a ger.

Fuel is in Dzuunharaa, about thirty-four kilometres from the valley, and there is none in the hills, so fill up and carry spare. The best time is July and August, when the roads are dry and the grass is green. If you are lucky, a family will offer you fermented mare's milk, which is an acquired taste, or a bowl of noodle soup, and the hospitality is generous.
t.eastfjords coastal road point 2@64.7,-14:
Djúpivogur is a small village on the Eastfjords coast, tucked beneath a mountain that looks like it was made by a child with a pencil and a ruler. Búlandstindur rises almost a kilometre in a perfect pyramid, and the village at its foot has a quiet, unhurried air that makes it the kind of place you plan to stop for coffee and stay for the afternoon. It has been a trading post for centuries, and the old warehouse by the harbour, built in the late eighteenth century, is among the oldest buildings in the region.

The riding to Djúpivogur is a highlight. The Ring Road swings around headland after headland, with sudden views across the fjords, and the bends are generally gentle but surprising, with a few narrow bridges and short climbs. The surface is generally good, but the weather can turn quickly, and fog rolls in from the sea. Take care on the open sections, since the wind can be fierce. Beyond the village, a mountain road called Öxi cuts inland toward Egilsstaðir, a rough, steep, gravel shortcut that is better left to those with suitable bikes and good weather.

What sets the village apart is a row of granite eggs on the shore of the little bay called Gleðivík, thirty-four of them, each one a different size, each modelled on the egg of a local bird. It is a modern piece of public art, and the effect, in the pale light of an evening, is quietly moving. The village also prides itself on being a slow town, a member of an international network that favours local food and a relaxed pace, and it shows in the way people talk to visitors.

Nature is rich. Offshore lies the island of Papey, home to puffins and other seabirds, with boat trips in summer, and the fjord holds seals and whales. The air smells of kelp and cold water, and the mountains glow rose-pink at sunset.

The village is small, with a shop, a cafe and a few places to stay, and larger services are found farther along the Ring Road. Come in the late afternoon, take a walk along the shore, and stay for the light.

Breiðdalsvík is one of those East Iceland villages that feels as if the road has paused to catch its breath. It sits at the mouth of the Breiðdalur valley, a broad, green trough running inland between steep walls of dark rock, with a small harbour, a few streets and a population of a few hundred. The Eastfjords are the oldest part of Iceland, and the mountains here are layered like a stack of burnt toast, striped with the lava flows of millions of years.

For geologists, the valley is a treasure. A local centre named after a Scottish geologist who spent decades mapping the area tells the story of the ancient volcano that once stood here, whose eroded roots now form the colourful hills. You can read the rock like a book, with bands of red, ochre and black marking different eruptions. Even if you know nothing about geology, the colours are striking, especially in low sun.

The ride in is a pleasure. From the south the Ring Road winds around headland after headland, with sea cliffs and small bays, and the bends are gentle and open. From the north it comes through the valley of the Breiðdalur river, with farms and sheep and the occasional waterfall. The road is generally well kept, but there are single-lane bridges, so slow down and watch for oncoming traffic. Fog is common here in summer, and the temperature can drop fast.

The villagers live mainly from fishing and a little farming, and the harbour has a few small boats. A fish factory once dominated life here, and the old buildings of the district hint at a busier past. In summer there is a small cafe and a shop, with a certain charm about a place that is not trying too hard.

Larger settlements are some distance away, Reyðarfjörður and Eskifjörður to the north, so use the time here to walk and look. Bring a wind-proof layer, and expect the weather to change.
